# Movable-type printing press (`printing_press`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/communication.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Communication & information (`communication`)
- Deps: helped by paper, alphabet_writing, woodblock_printing, codex_book
- Core idea: European letterpress combines several techniques. (1) Type: a hardened steel punch is cut for each letter and struck into copper to make a matrix; the matrix sits in an adjustable hand mould into which type metal (lead with tin and antimony) is poured, giving thousands of identical letters of exactly the same height. (2) Ink: lampblack ground in boiled linseed-oil varnish, which clings to metal. (3) Press: a screw press like a wine or paper press presses dampened paper evenly on the inked type. Compositors set letters into lines and pages and redistribute them after printing. A two-man press made roughly 1,500 to 3,000 impressions in a long day.
- Pitfalls:
  - Saying Gutenberg invented printing: woodblock printing is some 600 years older and movable type had been made in China and Korea
  - Thinking the press was the hard part: the hand mould for casting exact type was the key step
  - Using water-based ink on metal type (it beads) or pure lead type (too soft, shrinks on cooling): antimony makes the alloy hard and sharp
  - Underestimating cost and market: paper was the largest expense and many early printers went bankrupt on unsold books
  - Repeating that the Ottomans banned printing in 1485 as settled fact: the decrees are known only from later European reports and the reasons for slow adoption are debated
- History: china: 1040s – Bi Sheng prints with baked-clay movable type (described by Shen Kuo, Mengxi bitan, 1088); c. 1297–1298 Wang Zhen's wooden type and rotating type tables; c. 1490 Hua Sui prints with bronze type in Wuxi; woodblock remains dominant; east_asia: 1377 – Jikji, printed with metal type at Heungdeok temple, Korea, the oldest surviving metal-type book (earlier Korean metal printing of 1234 is recorded but lost); 1403 royal type foundry; 1590s Japan; europe: c. 1440 – Gutenberg's experiments at Strasbourg; c. 1450 Mainz; 1454–1455 42-line Bible; 1465 Subiaco; 1469 Venice; 1471 Florence; by 1500 presses in some 250 towns; 1514 an Arabic Book of Hours printed with movable type at Fano; islamic: 1493 – Jewish press in Istanbul; 1727 Müteferrika's Ottoman Turkish press; 1822 Bulaq press in Egypt; india: 1556 – Jesuit press at Goa; americas: 1539 – Mexico City (Juan Pablos); 1640 Cambridge, Massachusetts
- Read:
  - Elizabeth L. Eisenstein, The Printing Revolution in Early Modern Europe (1983)
  - Lucien Febvre & Henri-Jean Martin, L’Apparition du livre (1958; English translation, The Coming of the Book, 1976)
  - Tsien Tsuen-hsuin, Paper and Printing, Science and Civilisation in China vol. 5 part 1 (1985)
